# Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny

This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for an area
around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town is surrounded by
mountains, whose steep slopes are challenging terrain for SAR. The tutorial
compares the single-pass composites, one of the ascending and one of the
descending acquisitions, with a composite that combines both by local
resolution weighting (LRW).

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv

root = next(p for p in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents) if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists())
load_dotenv(root / ".env")
(root / "cache/docs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
os.chdir(root / "cache/docs")
```

## Find the bursts in the area of interest

The search finds the VV bursts that overlap the area's grid square in a 12-day
window, 2025-08-13 to 2025-08-24. The area lies in one 10 km square of the MGRS
grid, and the search covers the entire square, as in
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#find-the-bursts-of-every-square):

```{python}
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data/martigny")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
aoi = box(7.01, 46.09, 7.055, 46.125)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-13", "2025-08-24")
(square,) = MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20)  # the area lies in one square
print(square.mgrs_code, square.crs)

search_area = box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox)
found = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))
bursts = found.intersecting(square)

bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg(
    acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()),
    bursts=("burst_id", "size"),
    sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))),
    satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))),
)
```

One ascending and two descending orbits cover the square, each imaged twice
in these 12 days, with 14 bursts in total.

## Process backscatter

The bursts are processed in the UTM zone of the square, at 20 m grid spacing:

```{python}
#| output: false
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=square.crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure().products
```

## Compose the composites

To compare local resolution weighting with single-pass composites, the square
is composed both ways. `compose_rtc_lrw()` combines both pass directions and
also writes the quality layers, and `compose_rtc_by_pass()` averages each
direction on its own, without weights. For an area of several squares,
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#compose-each-square) loops
over them.

```{python}
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
lrw = weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
by_pass = weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(rtc, square, time_range=window)
```

## Compare the composites

How finely a slope is resolved depends on how it faces the sensor. Sentinel-1
looks sideways, to the right of its track: east on ascending passes, west on
descending ones. Slopes facing the sensor are compressed by foreshortening or
layover and poorly resolved, while slopes facing away are well resolved or, if
steep enough, fall into radar shadow, where that pass direction has no value
([Why mountains need it](resolution-weighting.qmd#why-mountains-need-it)).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Backscatter composites of 2025-08-13 to 2025-08-24 in a 4 by 4 km window west of Martigny: the two ascending acquisitions (left), the four descending acquisitions (middle), and all six combined by local resolution weighting (right). White marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from s1bursts.product import Layer


def read(composite, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT):
    """Read one layer of a composite, with its extent in kilometers for imshow."""
    with fm.open(composite, layer) as src:
        left, bottom, right, top = (v / 1000 for v in src.bounds)
        return src.read(1).astype("float32"), [left, right, bottom, top]


view = (346, 350, 5106, 5110)  # easting and northing in km, UTM zone 32N
composites = {
    "Ascending": read(by_pass["Ascending"]),
    "Descending": read(by_pass["Descending"]),
    "LRW": read(lrw),
}
viridis = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
viridis.set_bad("white")  # pixels without a value: radar shadow

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, (data, extent)) in zip(axes, composites.items()):
    image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=extent, cmap=viridis, vmin=-15, vmax=0)
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.5, label="Backscatter (dB)")
plt.show()
```

Each single-pass composite has gaps where the steepest slopes facing away from
the sensor fall into radar shadow, and compresses the slopes facing it into
coarse streaks. The resolution-weighted composite averages all six
acquisitions but gives the better-resolved ones more weight, so it has a value
everywhere in this window, and its resolution varies less from slope to slope.

## Check quality layers

The LRW composite comes with two quality layers, shown here for the same
window:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Quality layers of the resolution-weighted composite (left): the number of acquisitions per pixel (middle) and the local resolution (right), darkest where the ground is most coarsely resolved."
# title: (layer, colorbar label, colormap, colorbar ticks, the first and last being the limits)
layers = {
    "LRW composite": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, "Backscatter (dB)", "viridis", [-15, -10, -5, 0]),
    "Observations": (Layer.QA_NUM, "Number of observations", "cividis", [0, 2, 4, 6]),
    "Quality": (Layer.QA_CQM, "Local resolution (dB)", "cividis", [-12, -8, -4, 0, 4, 8]),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.9), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (title, (layer, label, cmap, ticks)) in zip(axes, layers.items()):
    data, extent = read(lrw, layer)
    if layer != Layer.QA_NUM:
        data = 10 * np.log10(data)
    image = ax.imshow(data, extent=extent, cmap=cmap, vmin=ticks[0], vmax=ticks[-1])
    fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, orientation="horizontal", label=label, ticks=ticks)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
plt.show()
```

The number of observations (`QA-NUM`) counts the acquisitions outside radar
shadow that contribute to each pixel: all six almost everywhere, fewer where
one pass direction is in shadow. The composite quality map (`QA-CQM`) is the
local resolution of the composite itself. It is highest on slopes that face
away from the sensor in some orbits, and lowest on the steepest slopes, which
every orbit either compresses or leaves in shadow. A pixel with a low quality
describes the ground more coarsely than its 20 m grid spacing suggests.
[Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains both layers.
